questions.prompt: By Gauss's law the electric field between the plates is \(E = \sigma\varepsilon_0\).
questions.explanation: False — Eq. (ii) in the derivation of C.

questions.prompt: When K⁺ ions diffuse out of a nerve cell, a net negative charge is left inside the cell.
questions.explanation: True — Loss of positive ions leaves the inside negative.

questions.prompt: The net charge on a charged capacitor is zero.
questions.explanation: True — +Q on one plate and −Q on the other cancel.

questions.prompt: As charge builds up on the plates it repels more of the charge that is arriving, so the current drops.
questions.explanation: True — This explains the exponential behaviour.

questions.prompt: A capacitor stores energy in the form of an electric field.
questions.explanation: True — Energy is stored as electric potential energy.

questions.prompt: For a very small step in the derivation, \(r^2\) is taken as \(r_{N-1}r_N\).
questions.explanation: True — r_N and r_(N−1) are very close, so r² = r_(N−1) r_N.

questions.prompt: A free positive charge between two oppositely charged parallel plates moves from the positive plate to the negative plate and gains kinetic energy.
questions.explanation: True — The field points from the positive to the negative plate.

questions.prompt: Equivalent capacitance: membrane that lets some ions pass and blocks others.
questions.explanation: False — Equivalent capacitance: single capacitor that can replace a combination; the statement describes semipermeable membrane.

questions.prompt: The time constant of an RC circuit is \(\tau = R/C\).
questions.explanation: False — τ = RC.

questions.prompt: A farad is a volt per coulomb.
questions.explanation: False — 1 F = 1 C/V.

questions.prompt: Capacitor: electric currents or voltages in biological processes.
questions.explanation: False — Capacitor: device that stores electric energy; the statement describes bioelectricity.

questions.prompt: After one time constant, a discharging capacitor retains 36.7 % of its initial charge.
questions.explanation: True — Q = Q₀e⁻¹ = 0.367 Q₀.

questions.prompt: When the test charge is brought from infinity, \(1/r_N\) becomes zero in the derivation.
questions.explanation: True — r_N = ∞, so 1/r_N = 0.

questions.prompt: The energy stored in a capacitor is \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}CV^2\).
questions.explanation: True — Substitute Q = CV.

questions.prompt: Capacitance: animals that generate electric shocks.
questions.explanation: False — Capacitance: ability of a capacitor to store charge (Q/V); the statement describes electrogenic animals.

questions.prompt: Action potential: ability of a capacitor to store charge (Q/V).
questions.explanation: False — Action potential: electrical pulse produced in a stimulated cell; the statement describes capacitance.

questions.prompt: In a rectification circuit a capacitor acts to increase the ripple voltage.
questions.explanation: False — Smoothing the rectified output.

questions.prompt: Dielectric: insulating medium between the plates.
questions.explanation: True — The insulating medium (air or a sheet of some insulator) between the plates of a capacitor.

questions.prompt: Potential gradient: energy needed to move a charge against an electric field.
questions.explanation: False — Potential gradient: rate of change of potential with displacement; the statement describes electric potential energy.

questions.prompt: The potential energy of two point charges is inversely proportional to the distance between them.
questions.explanation: True — U = Qq/(4πε₀r).

questions.prompt: \(U_A - U_B = W_{BA}\) is the change in potential energy equals work done.
questions.explanation: True — Change in potential energy equals work done: \(U_A - U_B = W_{BA}\).

questions.prompt: Electrogenic animals: animals that generate electric shocks.
questions.explanation: True — Animals that can naturally generate external electric shocks through internal biological mechanisms that act as batteries.

questions.prompt: Echidnas and platypuses are the best-known electrogenic animals.
questions.explanation: False — Electroreceptive examples in the textbook.

questions.prompt: The energy stored in a capacitor is \(E = \dfrac{2Q^2}{C}\).
questions.explanation: False — Substitute V = Q/C.

questions.prompt: Relative permittivity is \(\varepsilon_r = C_{med}/C_{vac}\).
questions.explanation: True — Eq. (19.8).

questions.prompt: In an electric fan a capacitor is used to stop the fan from turning.
questions.explanation: False — Textbook list of applications.

questions.prompt: \(\Delta V = \dfrac{\Delta U}{q_0}\) is the potential difference from potential energy.
questions.explanation: True — Potential difference from potential energy: \(\Delta V = \dfrac{\Delta U}{q_0}\).

questions.prompt: Potential difference is the work done in moving a unit positive charge from one point to another, keeping the charge in electrostatic equilibrium.
questions.explanation: True — Potential difference = work per unit positive charge.

questions.prompt: Ion channels are carbohydrates that let all molecules pass freely through the membrane.
questions.explanation: False — Proteins form the channels.

questions.prompt: RC circuit: circuit containing a resistor and a capacitor.
questions.explanation: True — A circuit containing a resistor and a capacitor, used to charge or discharge the capacitor through the resistor.
False — micro means 10⁻⁶; milli means 10⁻³.

questions.prompt: Bacteria, yeast and fish can never be electrogenic.
questions.explanation: False — Electric eels are the best known, not the only ones.

questions.prompt: The change in potential energy of a charge is given by \(\Delta U = q_0\,\Delta V\).
questions.explanation: True — From \(\Delta V = \Delta U/q_0\) we get \(\Delta U = q_0\Delta V\).

questions.prompt: 1 kV equals \(10^{3}\) V.
questions.explanation: True — kilo means 10³.

questions.prompt: \(Q_0 = C\varepsilon\) is the maximum charge while charging.
questions.explanation: True — Maximum charge while charging: \(Q_0 = C\varepsilon\).

questions.prompt: \(E = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\) is the two capacitors in series.
questions.explanation: False — Two capacitors in series is \(C_e = \dfrac{C_1C_2}{C_1+C_2}\); \(E = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\) is the energy stored from charge and capacitance.

questions.prompt: A capacitor takes a longer time than a battery to charge up.
questions.explanation: False — Textbook 'For Your Information' box.

questions.prompt: A capacitor can release all of its energy very quickly.
questions.explanation: True — This is why it is used in camera flashes.

questions.prompt: \(\Delta U = q_0\,\Delta V\) is the capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric.
questions.explanation: False — Capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor with a dielectric is \(C_{med} = \dfrac{A\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r}{d}\); \(\Delta U = q_0\,\Delta V\) is the change in potential energy of a charge.

questions.prompt: In a parallel combination every capacitor has the same voltage across it.
questions.explanation: True — The battery supplies the same V to each.

questions.prompt: Ion channels are proteins on the cell surface that let certain ions pass through the membrane.
questions.explanation: True — Proteins form the channels.

questions.prompt: In a series combination every capacitor carries the same charge.
questions.explanation: True — Electrostatic induction makes Q the same on each.

questions.prompt: Na⁺, K⁺, Ca²⁺ and Cl⁻ ions diffuse through ion channels down their electrochemical gradients.
questions.explanation: True — Specific inorganic ions use ion channels.

questions.prompt: Sharks and rays cannot detect electric fields.
questions.explanation: False — They detect electricity.

questions.prompt: The capacitance of a parallel plate capacitor depends on the plate area, the plate separation and the medium between the plates.
questions.explanation: True — C = Aε₀ε_r/d.

questions.prompt: An ion channel forms a hydrophobic tunnel across the membrane.
questions.explanation: False — Hydrophilic tunnels allow ions through by diffusion.

questions.prompt: \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\) is the potential difference in a constant field.
questions.explanation: False — Potential difference in a constant field is \(\Delta V = -E\,\Delta r\); \(E = \dfrac{V}{d}\) is the field between the plates (from potential).

questions.prompt: Nerve-cell and muscle-cell membranes are slightly permeable only to chloride ions.
questions.explanation: False — K⁺ diffuses outward.

questions.prompt: A capacitor is a device used to store electric energy.
questions.explanation: True — Capacitors store energy in the form of an electric field.

questions.prompt: The electric potential due to a point charge decreases as the distance from the charge increases.
questions.explanation: True — V ∝ 1/r.

questions.prompt: In deriving the potential due to a point charge, the path is divided into small steps so that the force becomes zero in each step.
questions.explanation: False — E varies as 1/r², so it is taken constant only over a tiny step.

questions.prompt: The capacitance of a capacitor is \(C = QV\).
questions.explanation: False — C = Q/V.

questions.prompt: The maximum charge on a charging capacitor is \(Q_0 = C\varepsilon\).
questions.explanation: True — Maximum charge = capacitance × e.m.f.

questions.prompt: The charge stored on a capacitor is directly proportional to the voltage applied across it.
questions.explanation: True — Q ∝ V, so Q = CV.

questions.prompt: A battery stores electrical energy and releases it through chemical reactions.
questions.explanation: True — A capacitor, not a battery, uses plates.

questions.prompt: A capacitor can release all of its energy only very slowly.
questions.explanation: False — This is why it is used in camera flashes.

questions.prompt: Capacitors are used in radio and TV sets to filter unwanted frequencies.
questions.explanation: True — Filtering is a standard role.

questions.prompt: The electric potential at a point equals the work done in bringing a unit positive charge from infinity to that point.
questions.explanation: True — Infinity is the reference point where the potential is zero.

questions.prompt: The unit of electric potential is the joule per coulomb, which is called the volt.
questions.explanation: True — 1 V = 1 J/C.

questions.prompt: \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}QV\) is the equivalent capacitance in series.
questions.explanation: False — Equivalent capacitance in series is \(\dfrac{1}{C_e} = \dfrac{1}{C_1}+\dfrac{1}{C_2}+\dfrac{1}{C_3}\); \(E = \tfrac{1}{2}QV\) is the energy stored from charge and voltage.

questions.prompt: In a parallel combination the capacitors are connected between the same two points.
questions.explanation: True — Parallel = same two points.

questions.prompt: Electric potential energy: single capacitor that can replace a combination.
questions.explanation: False — Electric potential energy: energy needed to move a charge against an electric field; the statement describes equivalent capacitance.

questions.prompt: N identical capacitors C connected in series have an effective capacitance \(C/N\).
questions.explanation: True — 1/Ce = N/C.

questions.prompt: The equation \(x = x_0\,e^{-t/RC}\) can describe only the charge of a discharging capacitor.
questions.explanation: False — x may be current, charge or potential difference (Eq. 19.15).

questions.prompt: The equivalent capacitance of parallel capacitors is smaller than the smallest individual capacitance.
questions.explanation: False — Eq. (19.10).

questions.prompt: To store a large amount of energy in a capacitor bank, the capacitors should be connected in parallel.
questions.explanation: True — Parallel gives the largest equivalent capacitance.

questions.prompt: Echidnas and platypuses are electroreceptive animals.
questions.explanation: True — Electroreceptive examples in the textbook.

questions.prompt: Capacitors in camera flashes convert light directly into chemical energy.
questions.explanation: False — Flash guns need a sudden burst of energy.

questions.prompt: Potential difference is the force exerted on a unit charge at one of the two points.
questions.explanation: False — Potential difference = work per unit positive charge.

questions.prompt: Time constant: time to reach 63.2 % of the maximum charge (RC).
questions.explanation: True — The time during which 63.2 % of the maximum charge is deposited on the plates of the capacitor in an RC circuit; it equals RC.

questions.prompt: Resting potential: about 50 mV across a cell membrane.
questions.explanation: True — The bioelectric potential across a cell membrane, typically about 50 millivolts.

questions.prompt: The electric potential at distance r from a point charge Q is \(V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\).
questions.explanation: True — V = U/q ∝ 1/r (Eq. 19.5).

questions.prompt: \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\) is the capacitance of a capacitor.
questions.explanation: True — Capacitance of a capacitor: \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\).

questions.prompt: While charging, the voltage on the capacitor is initially zero and rises rapidly at first.
questions.explanation: True — Initial current is maximum, so the voltage grows fastest at first.

questions.prompt: When a battery charges a capacitor, equal and opposite charges +Q and −Q appear on its two plates.
questions.explanation: True — Equal amounts of positive and negative charge are separated onto the plates.

questions.prompt: During discharging, \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\).
questions.explanation: True — Charge decays exponentially.

questions.prompt: \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\) is the discharging of a capacitor.
questions.explanation: True — Discharging of a capacitor: \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\).

questions.prompt: For capacitors in parallel, \(C_e = C_1 + C_2 + C_3\).
questions.explanation: True — Add the capacitances directly in parallel.

questions.prompt: \(U_A - U_B = W_{BA}\) is the energy stored from charge and capacitance.
questions.explanation: False — Energy stored from charge and capacitance is \(E = \dfrac{Q^2}{2C}\); \(U_A - U_B = W_{BA}\) is the change in potential energy equals work done.

questions.prompt: \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\) is the field between the plates (gauss's law).
questions.explanation: False — Field between the plates (Gauss's law) is \(E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}\); \(C = \dfrac{Q}{V}\) is the capacitance of a capacitor.

questions.prompt: The cell membrane is completely impermeable to all ions.
questions.explanation: False — Selective passage of ions.

questions.prompt: The charging of a capacitor through a resistor is linear with time.
questions.explanation: False — Q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

questions.prompt: N identical capacitors C connected in series have an effective capacitance \(NC\).
questions.explanation: False — 1/Ce = N/C.

questions.prompt: The equation \(x = x_0\,e^{-t/RC}\) can describe the current, charge or potential difference of a discharging capacitor.
questions.explanation: True — x may be current, charge or potential difference (Eq. 19.15).

questions.prompt: Most electrogenic animals are also electroreceptive.
questions.explanation: True — But many electroreceptive animals are not electrogenic.

questions.prompt: The charging of a capacitor through a resistor is exponential, not linear.
questions.explanation: True — Q = Q₀(1 − e^(−t/RC)).

questions.prompt: While a capacitor is charging, the current is highest at the start.
questions.explanation: True — Current falls gradually to zero.

questions.prompt: A battery stores electrical energy by distributing charged particles on two plates.
questions.explanation: False — A capacitor, not a battery, uses plates.

questions.prompt: A concentration imbalance of ions across a membrane gives rise to an electric potential difference.
questions.explanation: True — Equal and opposite net charges are produced in the two solutions.

questions.prompt: A farad is a coulomb per volt.
questions.explanation: True — 1 F = 1 C/V.

questions.prompt: Capacitors in camera flashes store and quickly release a large amount of electrical energy.
questions.explanation: True — Flash guns need a sudden burst of energy.

questions.prompt: A capacitor stays charged after the battery is removed because the dielectric becomes a battery.
questions.explanation: False — Mutual attraction keeps the charges bound.

questions.prompt: The equivalent capacitance of series capacitors is less than any individual capacitance.
questions.explanation: True — Eq. (19.9).

questions.prompt: Dielectric: about 50 mV across a cell membrane.
questions.explanation: False — Dielectric: insulating medium between the plates; the statement describes resting potential.

questions.prompt: Semipermeable membrane: charge per unit area of a plate.
questions.explanation: False — Semipermeable membrane: membrane that lets some ions pass and blocks others; the statement describes surface charge density.

questions.prompt: \(\Delta V = -E\,\Delta r\) is the potential difference in a constant field.
questions.explanation: True — Potential difference in a constant field: \(\Delta V = -E\,\Delta r\).

questions.prompt: In deriving the potential due to a point charge, the path is divided into small steps so that the electric field is nearly constant in each step.
questions.explanation: True — E varies as 1/r², so it is taken constant only over a tiny step.

questions.prompt: Some types of bacteria, yeast and fish are also electrogenic.
questions.explanation: True — Electric eels are the best known, not the only ones.

questions.prompt: A smaller time constant means slower charging and discharging.
questions.explanation: False — τ = RC sets the speed.

questions.prompt: Parallel combination: capacitors joined between the same two points.
questions.explanation: True — Capacitors connected between the same two points.

questions.prompt: Bringing a charge q from infinity to distance r from a charge Q gives a potential energy \(U = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r^2}\).
questions.explanation: False — U ∝ 1/r (Eq. 19.4).

questions.prompt: Relative permittivity: ratio of capacitance with a dielectric to that in vacuum.
questions.explanation: True — The ratio of the capacitance of a capacitor with a dielectric between the plates to the capacitance of the same capacitor when the space is evacuated.

questions.prompt: \(\varepsilon_r = \dfrac{C_{med}}{C_{vac}}\) is the equivalent capacitance in parallel.
questions.explanation: False — Equivalent capacitance in parallel is \(C_e = C_1+C_2+C_3\); \(\varepsilon_r = \dfrac{C_{med}}{C_{vac}}\) is the relative permittivity.

questions.prompt: The graph of potential difference against charge for a capacitor is a straight line through the origin.
questions.explanation: True — V = Q/C is linear in Q.

questions.prompt: \(\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{A}\) is the change in potential energy of a charge.
questions.explanation: False — Change in potential energy of a charge is \(\Delta U = q_0\,\Delta V\); \(\sigma = \dfrac{Q}{A}\) is the surface charge density of a plate.

questions.prompt: During discharging, the charge −Q on the negative plate flows through the resistance and neutralises the charge +Q on the positive plate.
questions.explanation: True — The switch is at terminal 2.

questions.prompt: \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\) is the charge stored on a capacitor.
questions.explanation: False — Charge stored on a capacitor is \(Q = CV\); \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\) is the discharging of a capacitor.

questions.prompt: In the charging and discharging equations the constant \(e\) is about 3.1416.
questions.explanation: False — e ≈ 2.7182.

questions.prompt: Electric potential at a point depends on the size of the test charge placed there.
questions.explanation: False — A test charge of any size has the same electric potential at a given location.

questions.prompt: Electric potential energy is the energy needed to move a charge against an electric field.
questions.explanation: True — Moving a charge against the field requires energy; that energy is the electric potential energy.

questions.prompt: 1 mF equals \(10^{-3}\) F.
questions.explanation: True — milli = 10⁻³.

questions.prompt: In a series combination, all the right plates are joined to one common point.
questions.explanation: False — Series = plate to plate.

questions.prompt: A computer chip contains a number of capacitors.
questions.explanation: True — Capacitors are a common component of electronic devices.

questions.prompt: All points at the same distance from an isolated source charge are at the same electric potential.
questions.explanation: True — V depends only on r.

questions.prompt: The maximum charge on a charging capacitor is \(Q_0 = \varepsilon/C\).
questions.explanation: False — Maximum charge = capacitance × e.m.f.

questions.prompt: During charging, \(Q = Q_0\,e^{-t/RC}\).
questions.explanation: False — The discharging law is Q₀e^(−t/RC).

questions.prompt: Relative permittivity is \(\varepsilon_r = C_{vac}/C_{med}\).
questions.explanation: False — Eq. (19.8).

questions.prompt: In a series combination, the right plate of one capacitor is connected to the left plate of the next.
questions.explanation: True — Series = plate to plate.

questions.prompt: One farad is a very large capacitance.
questions.explanation: True — 1 C is a very large charge; typical capacitors are pF to mF.

questions.prompt: \(U = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) is the relative permittivity.
questions.explanation: False — Relative permittivity is \(\varepsilon_r = \dfrac{C_{med}}{C_{vac}}\); \(U = \dfrac{Qq}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 r}\) is the potential energy of two point charges.

questions.prompt: A discharging capacitor is fully discharged when the current is at its maximum.
questions.explanation: False — No current means no charge is stored.

questions.prompt: Bringing the plates of a parallel plate capacitor closer together increases its capacitance.
questions.explanation: True — C ∝ 1/d.

questions.prompt: Electroreception is the ability to detect weak, naturally occurring electrostatic fields in the environment.
questions.explanation: True — Detection, not generation.
